title: Future Trends and Climate Change
quiz.0.question: What is the most direct and widespread effect of global warming on the style of Italian wine?
quiz.0.options.0: Wines are getting paler and paler
quiz.0.options.1: Wines are becoming extremely acidic and hard to drink
quiz.0.options.2: Grapes ripen earlier, raising alcohol and making fruit riper or jammy
quiz.0.options.3: Strong oaky vanilla appears in the wine
quiz.0.explanation: Higher temperatures make sugar build up too fast in the grapes, turning into higher alcohol after fermentation; at the same time acidity is lost and the fruit shifts from fresh to ripe or even jammy.
quiz.1.question: To cope with the heat brought by climate change, which is one of the most common vineyard-management adaptations by Italian estates?
quiz.1.options.0: Cutting down trees around the vines to increase sunlight
quiz.1.options.1: Changing canopy management, keeping more leaves to shade the grapes and prevent sunburn
quiz.1.options.2: Replanting entirely with thirsty international grapes such as Chardonnay
quiz.1.explanation: Growers used to strip leaves to help grapes ripen; now, to prevent extreme heat from burning the grapes (sunburn), they keep more leaves as a "parasol".
quiz.2.question: In traditional Barolo, which exposure did the most expensive vineyards usually have? Under climate change, which exposures are estates reassessing?
quiz.2.options.2: Formerly south-facing for the most sun; now reassessing east- or north-facing to avoid overexposure
quiz.2.options.3: Formerly flat land; now reassessing valley floors
quiz.2.explanation: Traditionally Nebbiolo needed plenty of sun to ripen, so south-facing slopes were most prized. But in extremely hot years, south-facing slopes easily lead to over-ripe or sunburnt grapes, so cooler east- or north-facing slopes are gaining attention.
quiz.3.question: Italian estates have adjusted their winemaking in response to climate change. Which of these is NOT a common strategy?
quiz.3.options.0: Early harvest to preserve the grapes' natural acidity
quiz.3.options.1: Using fewer new small barrels (barriques) in favour of large old casks or concrete to keep the fruit fresh
quiz.3.options.2: Keeping some stems during red fermentation (whole-bunch fermentation) for freshness and structure
quiz.3.options.3: Adding lots of sugar before fermentation (chaptalisation) to raise alcohol
quiz.3.explanation: Climate change has already pushed sugar too high and alcohol soaring, so estates aim to "lower" alcohol and keep acidity, and would never add more sugar (Italy already bans adding sucrose, allowing enrichment only with concentrated grape must).
slides.0.title: Future Trends and Climate Change
slides.0.subtitle: The age of warming: transformation strategies and the future map of Italian wine
slides.1.title: Four Direct Impacts of Climate Change
slides.1.content:
🌡️ Rising temperatures

The most direct structural threat

Average summer temperatures in Italy have risen markedly over the past 30 years; grapes ripen earlier, sugar builds up too fast and acidity is lost; many Barolos now commonly reach 14.5-15% alcohol, and Amarone even higher

💧 Drought and water shortage

The threat of water stress

Less winter snow and long rainless summers; vines face severe water stress, affecting yield and quality; top areas that long banned irrigation have begun discussing allowing emergency drip irrigation

⛈️ More frequent extreme weather

Unpredictable catastrophic risks

Spring frost, violent summer hail and storms are more frequent and harder to predict; they can destroy a whole year's crop overnight, and insurance costs have soared

🍷 Impact on style and brand

A threat to Italian wine's core image

Ever-higher alcohol + ever-riper, jammy fruit; traditional freshness and elegance are fading; the "typical Italian style" consumers expect is being redefined
slides.2.title: Redrawing the Map: Moving Higher and Cooler
slides.2.content:
To find cooler conditions that preserve the grapes' acidity and elegance, Italian vineyards are undergoing a "great migration" that is rewriting the traditional map of wine areas.

⬆️ Moving to higher altitudes

  • The principle: temperature falls by about 0.6°C for every 100 m of altitude
  • Examples: Alto Adige (the Alps), Valle d'Aosta (Italy's highest vineyards), the upper slopes of Etna (800-1,000 m)
  • Strategy: estates are planting new vineyards on high sites once considered too cold
  • The Prosecco case: more and more producers seek the steep upper slopes of Valdobbiadene to keep their sparkling wines crisp

↖️ Moving to cooler exposures

  • An exposure revolution: traditionally Barolo's most expensive vineyards faced south to catch the most sun
  • Now: overexposure causes sunburn, so estates are valuing east- or north-facing slopes
  • A shift in latitude: Alto Piemonte (Gattinara, Ghemme), once considered "too cold", is now drawing more and more Nebbiolo producers
  • The cool-climate dividend: warming lets high-latitude/high-altitude areas grow grapes that once could not ripen
slides.3.title: Three Vineyard-Management Adaptation Strategies
slides.3.content:
Besides relocating vineyards, estates are actively adjusting vineyard management to soften the impact of climate change

☂️ Canopy management: growers used to strip leaves to expose grapes to the sun; now they keep more leaves as a "parasol" to protect the grapes from sunburn. Keeping leaves in summer markedly lowers berry temperature and effectively slows over-ripening
🌿 The revival of late-ripening grapes: replanting late-ripening, drought-tolerant native grapes that keep high acidity — Aglianico in the South (very late ripening) and the whites Fiano and Carricante (Etna, Sicily) have all gained in value as the climate warms
💧 Irrigation rules relaxed: many top European areas (such as Barolo) long banned irrigation, believing water stress drives roots deeper. Now, faced with extreme drought, the rules have begun to relax, allowing low-volume drip irrigation in emergencies
slides.4.title: Winemaking Adjustments and Regulatory Challenges
slides.4.content:
⏰ Early harvest

A key decision to preserve acidity

To keep acidity and avoid excessive alcohol, many estates pick 1-2 weeks earlier than tradition; sacrificing some fruit ripeness in exchange for a fresher structure

🪣 Less new small oak

From barriques to large vessels

Avoiding too many new small barrels (barriques) in favour of large old casks (botti), concrete tanks or amphorae; reducing oak extraction to keep the fruit fresh and avoid heaviness

🍇 Whole-bunch fermentation

A modern technique for freshness

Keeping the stems during red-wine fermentation, using their tannic structure and natural coolness to balance high alcohol; some estates are starting to experiment (still a minority with Nebbiolo)

📜 Regulatory dilemmas and the future

The DOC/DOCG adaptation challenge

Traditional rules fix grapes, yields and minimum alcohol, but climate change makes the old rules hard to sustain. Italy has launched sustainability certifications such as Equalitas and VIVA, covering carbon footprint and water management
slides.5.title: Key Takeaways
slides.5.points.0: Four impacts of climate change: rising temperatures → early ripening and high alcohol; drought and water shortage; extreme weather (hail/late frost); jammy style
slides.5.points.1: Alcohol is rising in Italian wine (Barolo commonly 14.5-15%, Amarone higher), challenging freshness and elegance
slides.5.points.2: Strategy one: move to higher altitudes (such as Etna, 800-1000 m) or cooler exposures (north-east facing)
slides.5.points.3: Barolo's traditionally most expensive exposure is south-facing; east/north-facing slopes are now being reassessed to avoid overexposure
slides.5.points.4: Canopy management: keeping more leaves as a parasol markedly lowers berry temperature and slows over-ripening
slides.5.points.5: Late-ripening native grapes (Aglianico, Fiano) are increasingly valued as the climate warms
slides.5.points.6: Winemaking adjustments: early harvest to keep acidity, less new oak, whole-bunch fermentation for freshness
slides.5.points.7: Note: chaptalisation is never a response — with warming, alcohol is already too high, and Italy already bans adding sugar (sucrose)

slides.6.questions.4.options.0: It completely ruins grape quality, forcing all estates to close
slides.6.questions.4.options.1: Better ripeness, allowing grapes that once struggled to ripen in the cold to be grown
